lessons.title: Case Study: Why the Rupee Fell From 74 to 83 in 2022

children.text: The rupee ended 2021 at 74.33 per dollar. On 20 October 2022 it touched a record low of 83.29, and it closed the year at 82.72, its worst annual performance since 2013. News channels blamed "the war," "the Fed" or "oil," depending on the day. All of them were right, and none of them was the whole story. This lesson is a full post-mortem of the rupee's 2022, using every tool from this chapter: interest rate gaps, the current account, capital flows, crude, the dollar index and RBI intervention. By the end, you will be able to diagnose any sharp rupee move the same way.

body.text: 2022 was not one shock. It was almost every rupee-negative force from this chapter firing in the same year. RBI spent tens of billions of dollars slowing the fall, but it could not stop a move driven by global forces.

body.title: Two headlines, one move
body.prompt: Some reports said the rupee fell 10.14% in 2022. Others said it fell 11.3%. Using 74.33 at the end of 2021 and 82.72 at the end of 2022, calculate the percentage rise in USD/INR, which is the dollar's gain against the rupee. Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Dollar's gain = 82.72 ÷ 74.33 minus 1 = 11.29%. The rupee's loss = 74.33 ÷ 82.72 minus 1 = minus 10.14%. Both headlines described the same move, just from different sides, exactly as you learned in Chapter 2.

cells: US Fed and the dollar
The Fed raised rates by 4.25 percentage points, from near zero to a 4.25% to 4.50% range. The dollar index peaked near 114.8 in late September.
A globally strong dollar dragged down almost every currency
Capital flows, crude and the dollar index
Interest rate gap
RBI hiked from 4.00% to 6.25%, less than the Fed. The India minus US policy rate gap fell from 3.75 to 1.75 percentage points.
Rupee assets became less rewarding relative to dollar assets
Interest rate differentials and the carry trade
Crude oil
Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February. Brent spiked to nearly $139 a barrel in March.
More dollars needed for every barrel India imports
Capital flows, crude and the dollar index
Current account
The deficit hit a record $36.4 billion, 4.4% of GDP, in July to September, with a goods trade deficit of $83.5 billion.
India's dollar spending far exceeded its dollar earnings
Inflation, trade deficits and the current account
FPI flows
FPIs sold a record of roughly ₹1.21 lakh crore of Indian equities over the year.
Portfolio money left India and bought dollars
Capital flows, crude and the dollar index
RBI
RBI sold dollars heavily for much of the year. Reserves fell from about $642 billion in September 2021 to about $524.5 billion in October 2022.
Slowed the fall, but could not reverse the forces
RBI intervention and forex reserves

body.title: The force that was missing
body.question: Which of these was NOT a major reason for the rupee's fall in 2022?
options: Aggressive US Fed rate hikes and a surging dollar index
A spike in crude oil after Russia invaded Ukraine
Indian inflation running far above US inflation
Record FPI selling of Indian equities
body.explanation: In 2022, US inflation was actually higher than India's. US CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June, while India's peaked at 7.79% in April. The inflation gap, which usually weighs on the rupee, did not work against it that year. The other three were all major drivers.

events.title: Russia invades Ukraine
events.description: Crude, gold and commodity prices jump. Global investors dump risky assets, including emerging-market shares.

events.title: Oil near $139, RBI sells heavily
events.description: Brent spikes to nearly $139 a barrel early in the month. RBI net sells $20.10 billion in the spot market in March to steady the rupee.

events.title: The Fed starts hiking
events.description: The US Fed makes its first rate hike of the cycle, beginning its most aggressive tightening in decades.

events.title: RBI's surprise hike
events.description: RBI raises the repo rate by 40 basis points to 4.40% in an unscheduled meeting, starting its own tightening cycle.

events.title: RBI opens the inflow taps
events.description: RBI eases rules to attract NRI deposits, foreign debt investment and external borrowing, then sets up a framework to settle trade in rupees.

events.title: Rupee crosses 80
events.description: USD/INR breaks above 80 for the first time. RBI net sells $19.05 billion in July alone.

events.title: Record current account deficit
events.description: The quarter's current account deficit hits $36.4 billion, 4.4% of GDP, later reported by RBI.

events.title: Dollar index peaks
events.description: The DXY hits a two-decade high near 114.8 as the Fed signals more hikes.

events.title: Record low of 83.29
events.description: The rupee breaks past 83. Forex reserves fall to about $524.5 billion around the same time.

events.title: Stabilisation
events.description: The dollar index eases, crude cools and RBI turns a net buyer of dollars. The rupee ends the year at 82.72.

body.title: RBI Net Dollar Sales in the Spot Market, Selected Months of 2022 ($ billion)
Adding up the defence
body.prompt: Using the chart, add up RBI's net spot dollar sales in March, June, July, August, September and October 2022: $20.10 billion, $3.70 billion, $19.05 billion, $4.30 billion, $10.36 billion and $0.92 billion. What is the total, in $ billion? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: 20.10 + 3.70 + 19.05 + 4.30 + 10.36 + 0.92 = $58.43 billion in just six months, and that excludes forward market operations. Yet over the same stretch the rupee still slid from about 75.8 to past 83. Heavy intervention bought time and prevented panic, but the direction was set by the Fed, the dollar, oil and FPI flows.

body.title: What RBI's July 2022 measures were designed to do

children.text: Selling reserves treats the symptom. In July 2022, RBI also went after the cause: not enough dollars coming in. Its package aimed to widen the inflow side of the balance of payments.
Banks were allowed to offer higher rates on fresh FCNR(B) and NRE deposits, and those deposits were temporarily exempted from reserve requirements.
Some limits on FPI investment in government and corporate bonds were relaxed.
The automatic route limit for companies borrowing abroad was raised temporarily.
A framework to invoice and settle exports and imports in rupees, reducing dollar demand over the long run.
Was 2022 a Rupee Crisis? Putting It in Context

body.title: 2013 vs 2022: two bad years, very different risks

columns.label: 2013 taper tantrum
points: Full-year current account deficit near 5% of GDP
India labelled one of the Fragile Five
Inflation high in India and low in the US
Needed emergency gold curbs and a special swap window to stabilise

columns.label: 2022 dollar surge
points: FY23 current account deficit about 2% of GDP, despite a record quarter
Reserves still above $520 billion at their lowest point
Most currencies fell against the dollar, not just India's
Stabilised as the dollar index and crude cooled late in the year

body.text: The rupee's 10% fall in 2022 was painful, but it was mainly a story of global dollar strength rather than an Indian crisis. The dollar index hit a two-decade high, and major currencies such as the Japanese yen, the British pound and the euro also fell sharply against the dollar during the year, even though they belong to rich countries with no capital controls. That distinction matters: a currency falling alongside its peers usually recovers its footing when the global driver fades, while a currency falling alone signals a problem at home.

body.label: India's current account deficit, July to September 2022
body.context: A record for a single quarter, driven by a goods trade deficit of $83.5 billion. The deficit for the full FY23 was much lower, at about 2% of GDP.

body.text: Hindsight makes 2022 look obvious. It was not. In October, with the rupee past 83 and reserves shrinking, extrapolating to 85 or 90 felt natural. Instead, the dollar index turned, crude cooled, and the rupee spent most of 2023 in a narrow range in the low 80s. Diagnosing why a currency moved is a learnable skill. Predicting where it goes next is far harder, which is why hedgers lock rates instead of guessing.

body.title: Is 2026 another 2022?
body.scenario: It is September 2026. USD/INR is near 95.5 after touching record lows. Brent crude is above $100. FPIs have sold ₹2.37 lakh crore of Indian equities this year, more than all of 2025. Markets are betting on a Fed rate hike, but the dollar index is around 99, far below its 2022 peak. RBI sold a record $53.13 billion in the spot market in FY26 and holds a record net short forward position, yet reserves are at a record $785.7 billion. India's current account deficit was 0.6% of GDP in FY26, and India's CPI inflation of 4.45% is roughly one percentage point above US inflation.
body.prompt: Using the 2022 diagnosis table as a template, compare 2026 with 2022 force by force. Which forces look similar, which look different, and is the 2026 rupee weakness more of a global dollar story or an India-specific story?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Crude oil: similar. Brent above $100 is a major rupee negative in both years.
2. FPI flows: similar, and larger in 2026. Equity outflows of ₹2.37 lakh crore by September exceed the full-year 2022 record of roughly ₹1.21 lakh crore.
3. US Fed: partly similar. Hike expectations are rising, but the Fed is not running a 2022-style cycle so far.
4. Dollar index: different. At about 99, the DXY is nowhere near its 2022 peak near 114.8, so 2026 is not a broad global dollar surge.
5. Current account: different. 0.6% of GDP is far smaller than 2022's record quarter.
6. Inflation: slightly worse for the rupee in 2026, since India's inflation is now above US inflation, unlike 2022.
7. RBI: similar approach, heavy intervention, but more use of forwards and inflow schemes, and larger headline reserves.
8. Conclusion: with the dollar index relatively subdued, 2026 looks more India-specific than 2022, driven mainly by crude and record FPI outflows rather than a global dollar surge. That makes FPI flows and oil the key variables to watch for any turnaround.

body.title: The worst since
body.textWithBlank: The rupee's 10.14% fall in 2022 was its worst annual performance since the taper tantrum year of ___.
body.explanation: 2013 was the year of the taper tantrum and the Fragile Five label, when the rupee hit a then record low of about 68.85.

body.title: Diagnose any sharp rupee move in six steps
steps: Measure the move from both sides: the rise in USD/INR and the fall in the rupee.
Check the dollar index. Did most currencies fall, or just the rupee?
Check crude oil and India's latest trade and current account data.
Check FPI equity and debt flows for the same period on NSDL.
Compare the RBI and US Fed rate paths and the change in the rate gap.
Check RBI's intervention data and reserves for signs of how hard it leaned against the move.

cards.definition: Fell from 74.33 to 82.72, a 10.14% loss and its worst year since 2013, with a record low of 83.29 in October.
4.25 percentage points of hikes, taking the Fed funds range to 4.25% to 4.50%.
A record $36.4 billion, or 4.4% of GDP, in July to September 2022.
Measures to attract NRI deposits, FPI debt and external borrowing, plus a framework for trade settlement in rupees.
If a currency falls with its peers, the driver is usually global. If it falls alone, the problem is usually domestic.
Explaining why a currency moved is learnable. Forecasting its next move is far harder.

points: The rupee fell from 74.33 to 82.72 in 2022, a 10.14% loss, with a record low of 83.29 in October.
Almost every rupee-negative force fired at once: Fed hikes, a surging dollar index, a narrowing rate gap, an oil spike, a record quarterly current account deficit and record FPI selling.
Inflation was the exception. US inflation ran higher than India's in 2022.
RBI sold $58.43 billion in just six months of 2022 and let reserves fall, which slowed the rupee's slide but could not stop it.
Major currencies like the yen, pound and euro also fell sharply as the dollar index hit a two-decade high, showing that 2022 was mainly a global dollar story, unlike India's 2013 crisis.
Use the same force-by-force checklist to diagnose any rupee move, and remember that diagnosis is easier than prediction.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Exchange rates, intervention figures and balance of payments data are from RBI, NSDL and market reports and may have been revised. Quarter-end rates in the chart are approximate.
